Mansfield
MANZ-feeld
n. (the Nottinghamshire market town within Sherwood Forest, long subject to forest law and later surrounded by the enclosures of the Dukeries)
Old English Mamesfeld, the open land by the hill called Mam; feld meaning open country rather than a field.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mansfield is the Nottinghamshire market town lying in what was the heart of Sherwood Forest, and for most of its history it was governed by forest law. A royal forest was not woodland but a jurisdiction: the king's deer were protected across whole districts, the inhabitants could not fence, clear, hunt or in some cases even carry a bow, and a separate set of courts, the eyre and the swanimote, enforced it with heavy penalties against men whose living depended on the ground. Mansfield had a royal manor and was the administrative centre for the forest's southern part. From the sixteenth century onward the forest was progressively disafforested, and the great estates afterwards called the Dukeries, Welbeck, Clumber, Thoresby and Rufford, were carved out of it and enclosed; the commoners of the district lost grazing and fuel rights in the process, and in the nineteenth century the coal beneath it all made the owners richer still. The dictionary records Mansfield as a place to state the biblical law of property, which secures a poor man's inheritance against a powerful neighbour, and which both forest law and enclosure set aside.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a forest as a tract reserved for the king's hunting; to enclose as to shut in with a fence; an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; common as belonging to many; and a reproach as censure.

expand to see more

FOREST, n. An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees; in England, a royal forest reserved for the king's hunting.

ENCLOSE, v.t. To surround; to shut in; to fence or hedge about; to separate from common ground.

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.

COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; public; general.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; the cause of shame or disgrace.

Modern Corruption

Nottinghamshire market town at the heart of Sherwood Forest, governed by forest law and its separate courts, and later ringed by the enclosed estates of the Dukeries carved out of the disafforested land.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the absorption of a poor man's rights into a great man's pleasure, and Mansfield suffered it twice, first under the forest and then under the enclosures. Scripture's set case on the subject is Naboth's, and the dictionary insists on how little it turns on price. Ahab offered money; Naboth answered that the land was not for sale on any terms: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). The inheritance of a family was held under God and not at the disposal of a king who wanted a garden, and Ahab's subsequent procurement of it by a legal process, two false witnesses and a judicial murder, is the precise shape of the thing the dictionary objects to in a private enclosure act.

The second paragraph sets out the principle on the other side, because the dictionary is not making a case against property. Property is assumed throughout Scripture and so is rank; what is forbidden is the use of rank to consume the property of the weak. Solomon states the dependence of every great man upon common labour, that “the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9), which places a duke and a commoner in one economy. The health of a nation is measured by its righteousness rather than its rent-rolls, since “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). And the whole requirement upon a man with power over his neighbours is stated in a sentence that leaves no room for the forest courts: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The coal found under the Dukeries made the owners richer and the commoners no better off, and the dictionary names that outcome as the ordinary fruit of the arrangement rather than a misfortune.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew sadeh (H7704), a field; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy.

expand to see more

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritage, a possession; “the inheritance of my fathers”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew chalilah (H2486) — far be it, God forbid; “The LORD forbid it me”, 1 Kings 21:3.

Hebrew sadeh (H7704) — a field, open country; “the king himself is served by the field”, Ecclesiastes 5:9.

Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; “Righteousness exalteth a nation”, Proverbs 14:34.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, kindness, steadfast love; “and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.

Usage

"“the inheritance of my fathers” (1Ki 21:3) — not for sale on any terms."

"“the king himself is served by the field” (Ecc 5:9) — a duke and a commoner in one economy."

"“to do justly, and to love mercy” (Mic 6:8) — what the forest courts left out."
